facts.summary: Wisconsin's minimum wage is $7.25 per hour, the same as the federal minimum wage.
facts.notes: Statute fixes the rate at $7.25; Wisconsin has not enacted increases above the federal floor. Verify no 2026 legislative change.

facts.summary: Wisconsin requires overtime at 1.5x the regular rate for hours worked over 40 in a week and imposes no daily overtime, mirroring federal law.
facts.sourceAgency: Wisconsin Dept of Workforce Development (Equal Rights Division)
facts.notes: No daily overtime requirement; weekly 40-hour threshold only. Salary/exemption tests track the federal FLSA.

declining to attend employer meetings on religious or political matters
facts.summary: The Wisconsin Fair Employment Act protects several classes beyond the federal set, including marital status, sexual orientation, arrest and conviction records, military service, and off-duty lawful product use.
facts.notes: Full WFEA list also includes federally covered bases (age, race, color, disability, sex, national origin). Listed here are the state additions beyond the federal set.

facts.summary: The Wisconsin Fair Employment Act covers employers with at least one employee, far lower than the federal 15-employee threshold under Title VII/ADA.
facts.notes: Definition of 'employer' reaches any person engaging in business employing at least one individual.

facts.summary: A discrimination complaint under the Wisconsin Fair Employment Act must be filed with the Equal Rights Division no more than 300 days after the alleged discrimination.
facts.notes: Matches the federal 300-day deadline available in deferral states; filed with DWD Equal Rights Division (the state FEPA).

facts.summary: An action to recover unpaid wages or other compensation for personal services must be commenced within 2 years after the cause of action accrues.
facts.notes: Two-year limitation for wage/salary recovery actions; separate exceptions may apply under sub. (2).

facts.summary: The Wisconsin Fair Employment Act makes it unlawful to retaliate against an employee for opposing a discriminatory practice or for filing a complaint, testifying, or assisting in a WFEA proceeding.
facts.notes: General anti-retaliation provision within the WFEA; separate whistleblower statutes exist for public employees (§§ 230.80-230.89) and health care workers (§ 146.997).

facts.value: next regular payday, or within 31 days of the last day worked, whichever is earlier
facts.summary: Whether an employee quits or is discharged, Wisconsin requires final wages to be paid in full no later than the date the employee would regularly have been paid under the employer's payroll schedule, or within 31 days of the last day worked, whichever is earlier.
facts.notes: Confirmed directly against the primary statute text. A 24-hour deadline applies instead if the separation is due to the employer's business closing, merging, or relocating (not independently verified this session).
